title: How LLMs work inside applications: tokens, context windows and model APIs
summary: A model reads a window of tokens and predicts the next one until a stop condition, and everything an application does with it, chat, tools and retrieval, is a request metered in tokens. This lesson sets the numbers the rest of the LLM applications module refers to: tokens, context windows, dated prices, caching multipliers and lifetimes, thinking tokens and rate limits, with one request costed with and without prompt caching.

blocks.text: Anthropic's own rate-limit example makes the caching point in throughput terms: with a 2,000,000 input-tokens-per-minute limit and an 80% cache hit rate, an organization can process 10,000,000 total input tokens per minute, because cached tokens do not count toward the limit.

blocks.caption: Anthropic's pricing page works the same arithmetic for a one-hour Managed Agents coding session on Claude Opus 5.5 with 50,000 input and 15,000 output tokens, with and without 40,000 cache reads.

blocks.text: Anthropic documents cache pre-warming for latency-sensitive applications: a request with max_tokens set to 0 reads the system prompt or tool definitions into the cache and returns at once with no output, so the first real user request is not the one that pays the miss. The pre-warm is billed as a normal cache write, so its breakpoint, thinking configuration and effort must match the follow-up requests or it writes an entry the real traffic never hits.

OpenAI recommends reserving at least 25,000 tokens for reasoning and visible output when starting with its reasoning models, then tuning from the reasoning_tokens a response reports, because a response can reach max_output_tokens before any visible text and still bill the input and the reasoning.

OpenAI reports that, in its internal tests, the Responses API improves cache utilization by 40% to 80% compared with Chat Completions, and recommends it for all new projects. The figures are OpenAI's own claim from internal tests, not an independent measurement.

subtopics.title: Tokens: the unit that is metered, limited and priced

blocks.text: A model does not read characters or words. A tokenizer splits text into tokens from a fixed vocabulary: a token can be a single character such as z or a whole word such as cat, and long words are broken into several tokens. Everything this lesson quotes is in tokens: the context window, the output cap, the rate limits and the bill.

How many tokens a text makes depends on the model's tokenizer, the language and the type of content, so the same text costs a different number of tokens on different models. The table collects the planning figures the vendors publish. Treat them as estimates: they come from different tokenizers, and even one vendor's own figures do not reduce to a single characters-per-token rule.

blocks.text: Images and documents are tokens too. A single Claude request can include up to 600 images or PDF pages, or 100 on models with a 200k window, and every response reports what the request consumed in its usage field.
Count, do not guess. Count each prompt with the model ID you will call before it ships, and log the usage object of every response afterwards. A count measured on one model is not valid for another.

subtopics.title: One request, one response: the API keeps no conversation

blocks.text: On the Claude Messages API each turn sends all previous conversation history plus the new user message, and the reply the model generates becomes part of the next turn's input. Your application keeps the conversation and sends it again, which is why input size, not only output size, grows as a conversation does. A request carries a model ID, a max_tokens cap on the output, the system prompt, the messages, optional tools and optionally an effort level; the response carries content blocks, a stop_reason and a usage object with the token counts.

Vendors differ in who holds the history, and they move their recommended surface. As of 2026-10, OpenAI recommends the Responses API for all new projects, keeps Chat Completions supported, and states that the Assistants API was sunset on August 26, 2026.

blocks.text: Every Claude model ID is a pinned snapshot, so an ID in your configuration does not change under you. The retirement date is Anthropic's commitment for the platforms it operates; Amazon Bedrock and Google Cloud set their own. This lesson's convention: pin the ID, record it with every call, and treat a model change as a release.

subtopics.title: Streaming and stop reasons: every way a call can end

blocks.text: The first diagram follows one streamed Claude request from send to the end of the stream, including the failures that can stop it. Solid arrows are calls, dashed arrows are events or replies the API sends back, and the Model lane is a drawing convenience: the documentation specifies the event and stop-reason contract, not the internals.

blocks.text: Branch on stop_reason before using any content: a reply cut off by max_tokens or by the window is a different outcome from a finished answer. The token counts in the usage of message_delta are cumulative, and a failure after streaming has begun arrives as an error event inside the stream, such as overloaded_error, which in a non-streaming call would be HTTP 529. On Claude 4.5 models and newer a request whose input plus max_tokens exceeds the window is accepted and ends with model_context_window_exceeded; if the input alone exceeds the window the API returns a 400.

subtopics.title: The context window: size, what fills it, and what to do when it fills

blocks.text: The context window is everything the model can reference while it generates, including the reply itself. It counts the system prompt, every message with its tool results, images and documents, the tool definitions and the output including thinking. Cached prefixes still count, because caching changes what you pay and not whether the tokens occupy the window. More context is not automatically better: accuracy and recall degrade as the token count grows, which Anthropic calls context rot.

blocks.text: Because the API resends the history, the window fills in a fixed order. The flow shows what goes in, which part is the cacheable prefix, and how each reply joins the history for the next turn.

edges.label: The whole window is the input

steps.caption: Tool definitions, then the system prompt: the prefix a cache can reuse.
Every earlier turn goes in again on every request.
Retrieved documents and tool results the application adds for this step.
Everything in the window is the model's input.
The reply, with any thinking, is capped by max_tokens.
The reply becomes history and is sent again next turn.

blocks.legend: Edges show data moving into and out of one request, not network calls; your application stores the history and sends it again, so the loop closes through it. Tools, then system, then messages is the order a Claude prefix is cached in s3; the window holds the whole request and the reply s4. Sources: s3, s4.

blocks.text: Billed input grows faster than the conversation does, because turn n sends everything before it again. The table counts that with one assumption: every request's input is n times 1,000 tokens at turn n, history plus the new message, with no caching.

blocks.caption: Input tokens billed over a conversation, assumption: 1,000 tokens added per turn, no caching.

blocks.text: When a conversation approaches the window, Anthropic's documentation names server-side compaction, which summarizes the earlier parts of the conversation on the server, as the primary strategy for long-running conversations and agentic workflows. As of 2026-10 it is in beta for Claude 4.6 and later models; context editing adds strategies that clear old tool results or old thinking blocks. Dropping or summarizing old turns in your own code is the same trade of detail for room.

subtopics.title: What a request costs: dated prices and the formula

blocks.text: Cost is the sum of four meters: input tokens not read from cache, tokens written to the cache, tokens read from the cache and output tokens, each at its own price per million tokens (MTok). Output tokens include thinking, and on every current Claude model in the table the output price is five times the input price.
cost = (uncached input × input price + cache writes × write price + cache reads × read price + output, thinking included, × output price) ÷ 1,000,000, with every price in USD per MTok.

subtopics.title: Prompt caching: multipliers, lifetimes and what breaks a hit

blocks.text: Prompt caching reuses the processed prefix of a prompt instead of computing it again. A cache read costs a fraction of the base input price, a cache write costs more than ordinary input, and the stored prefix lives for a limited time that every use refreshes. The cache covers tools, then system, then messages, up to the block marked with cache_control. OpenAI's reason it works: the cache keeps the model's key-value states for a reusable prefix.

blocks.caption: Claude cache multipliers on the base input price, as of 2026-10.

blocks.text: The lifetime is measured from the start of the request that wrote or read the entry, so a reply that streams for 4 minutes leaves about 1 minute for the next request.

blocks.caption: Claude and OpenAI caching side by side, as of 2026-10.

blocks.text: On Claude, a change at one level invalidates that level and every later one; switching fast mode, the thinking configuration or the effort level also invalidates the message blocks. A timestamp or other per-request text before the breakpoint means the prefix never matches, so every request pays a write and none gets a read. A cache entry exists only after the first response begins, so parallel requests that share a prefix should wait for the first.

Check usage after you add a breakpoint. input_tokens counts only what follows the last breakpoint; total input is cache_read_input_tokens plus cache_creation_input_tokens plus input_tokens. If both cache fields are 0, nothing was cached, usually because the prompt is under the minimum length; no error is returned.

subtopics.title: Thinking and reasoning tokens: billed as output, counted in the window

blocks.text: Reasoning models spend tokens thinking before they answer, so a request's output can be far larger than the visible reply. OpenAI says reasoning tokens are not visible through the API yet occupy the context window and are billed as output tokens, and Anthropic says thinking tokens are a subset of max_tokens, billed as output tokens and counted toward rate limits.

On Claude, thinking is adaptive: the model decides per request whether to think and how much, so a turn can carry no thinking block at all, and effort is the lever that steers it. You do not set a thinking token budget. max_tokens is a hard cap on thinking and reply together, effort is soft guidance with no guaranteed token count, and a max_tokens sized for a reply without thinking is often too small once thinking starts. Changing the effort level between requests invalidates the message cache.

blocks.text: OpenAI warns that the cap can bite before any visible text: when generated tokens reach the window or max_output_tokens the response is incomplete, and you pay for the input and the reasoning without a visible answer. Claude's remedy list is the same two moves: raise max_tokens or lower effort.

subtopics.title: Latency, rate limits and the levers you can pull

blocks.text: Time to first token (TTFT), the definition used here, is the wait between sending a request and the first token arriving. This lesson's working model, not a vendor claim: input is processed before the first token and output is produced one token after another, so input size drives TTFT and output length, thinking included, drives the rest. Anthropic lists relative latency per model and says actual latency depends on prompt length, output length and thinking effort, and both vendors list shorter input processing among the benefits of caching. The pages cited here give relative speed, not tokens per second, so measure both from your own client. For the general latency ladder see sd-numbers.

Anthropic limits requests per minute (RPM), input tokens per minute (ITPM) and output tokens per minute (OTPM) per organization and model class. For most models, input tokens and cache writes count toward ITPM and cache reads do not, and OTPM counts the tokens actually generated, so a high max_tokens costs no limit. A 429 is a limit; wait for retry-after when it is sent. The 429 for a monthly spend cap has no retry-after, and retrying fails until access resumes.

blocks.caption: Claude Messages API limits by tier, as of 2026-10. Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 have equal separate limits and share one row; Fable 5.x is limited separately.
Which lever to pull first. Measure the quality effect on your own evaluation set before shipping any of them.

worked_example.title: Worked example: one request with and without prompt caching, on Claude Sonnet 5.5

blocks.text: A support assistant sends the same prefix of tool definitions and system prompt with every request, plus a small part that changes. The table fixes every input: the prices are the pricing page's, the sizes and the request count are assumptions chosen to make the arithmetic concrete.

blocks.caption: Inputs to the example
rows: 100, each starting within 5 minutes of the previous one

blocks.title: The cost of one request, then of 100, with and without caching
items: The first cached request writes the prefix: 20,000 × $2.50 ÷ 1,000,000 = $0.05.
So the first cached request costs the write, $0.05, plus its 1,000 changing tokens, 1,000 × $2 ÷ 1,000,000 = $0.002, plus the output, $0.005: $0.057.
That is $0.057 - $0.047 = $0.01 more than an uncached request, the write premium.
Every later request inside the window reads the prefix: 20,000 × $0.10 ÷ 1,000,000 = $0.002.
So a request that hits the cache costs the read, $0.002, plus the 1,000 changing tokens, $0.002, plus the output, $0.005: $0.009.
One read saves 20,000 × ($2 - $0.10) ÷ 1,000,000 = $0.038, more than the $0.01 premium, so a 5-minute write pays off after one read.
A 1-hour write costs 20,000 × ($4 - $2) ÷ 1,000,000 = $0.04 more than uncached.
Two reads save 2 × $0.038 = $0.076, more than $0.04, while one read saves less, so a 1-hour write pays off after two reads.
The saving is $4.70 - $0.948 = $3.752, about 80% of the uncached bill.
Rate limits: a cached request adds 1,000 tokens to ITPM instead of 21,000, because cache reads do not count toward it on this model class.
Add thinking, assuming 3,000 thinking tokens per request billed as output: 3,000 × $10 ÷ 1,000,000 = $0.03.
So a cached request with thinking costs $0.009 + $0.03 = $0.039, and thinking is its largest line.

blocks.caption: The same arithmetic as code: the cost of one response from its usage object, with an explicit breakpoint at the end of the stable prefix.
blocks.code:
import anthropic

# USD per million tokens for claude-sonnet-5-5, as of 2026-10 (pricing page).
PRICE = {"input": 2.00, "cache_write_5m": 2.50, "cache_read": 0.10, "output": 10.00}


def request_cost(usage) -> float:
    """Cost of one Messages API response, from its usage object."""
    return (
        usage.input_tokens * PRICE["input"]
        + usage.cache_creation_input_tokens * PRICE["cache_write_5m"]
        + usage.cache_read_input_tokens * PRICE["cache_read"]
        + usage.output_tokens * PRICE["output"]  # thinking tokens are inside output_tokens
    ) / 1_000_000


client = anthropic.Anthropic()  # reads the API key from the environment

resp = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-5-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    # Explicit breakpoint at the end of the stable prefix. A top-level cache_control
    # (automatic caching) would mark the changing question instead: every request
    # would write the cache and none would read it.
    system=[{"type": "text", "text": SYSTEM_PROMPT, "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}}],
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": question}],
)

if resp.stop_reason != "end_turn":
    handle_stop_reason(resp.stop_reason)  # max_tokens, tool_use, refusal: see the stop reason table
print(request_cost(resp.usage))
